title: RIQUET A LA HOUPPE
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
source: Charles Perrault, « RIQUET A LA HOUPPE », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: Riquet with the Tuft is a tale of two gifts: a hideous prince who can give wit to the one he loves best, and a beautiful but stupid princess who can make handsome the one she loves. It belongs to the drawing rooms of Perrault’s day, where «esprit» ‘wit’, a quick and graceful mind, was prized as highly as looks, so the notes follow that word and the courtly language of compliments, suitors and promises. At the end the narrator offers two accounts of the transformation, the fairy’s gift or the eyes of love, and both verse morals come down on the side of love.

glossary.oüy: ouïr (ouï) — to hear (past participle; avoir oüy dire, to have heard said; 1697 spelling of ouï)

sentences.t: Il estoit une fois une Reine qui accoucha d’un fils, si laid & si mal fait, qu’on douta longtemps s’il avoit forme humaine.
sentences.say: Il était une fois une Reine qui accoucha d’un fils, si laid et si mal fait, qu’on douta longtemps s’il avait forme humaine.
sentences.l: There was one time a Queen who gave birth to a son, so ugly and so badly made, that one doubted for a long time whether he had human form.
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a Queen who gave birth to a son so ugly and so misshapen that for a long while people doubted whether he had human form at all.
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). «accoucha» ‘gave birth’ and «douta» ‘doubted’ are in the passé simple, the tense French keeps for telling a story: each verb names an event, complete in itself. Everyday speech has given it up for the passé composé («a accouché»), and English renders it with a plain past. «accoucher de» is ‘to be delivered of’ a child. «mal fait» ‘badly made’ is ‘ill-formed, misshapen’, and «avoit» is «avait» ‘had’, the same 1697 «oi» for modern «ai». «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’, and the capital on «Reine» ‘Queen’ is the printer’s too.

sentences.t: Une Fée, qui se trouva à sa naissance, asseura qu’il ne laisseroit pas d’estre aimable, parce qu’il auroit beaucoup d’esprit :
sentences.say: Une Fée, qui se trouva à sa naissance, assura qu’il ne laisserait pas d’être aimable, parce qu’il aurait beaucoup d’esprit :
sentences.l: A fairy, who found herself at his birth, assured that he would not fail to be lovable, because he would have much wit:
sentences.i: A fairy who was present at his birth declared that he would be lovable all the same, because he would have a great deal of wit.
sentences.n: «se trouva à sa naissance» ‘found herself at his birth’ is ‘was present at it’: in these tales fairies attend the births of princes to bestow their gifts. «asseura» is the 1697 spelling of «assura» ‘assured, declared’, another passé simple. «ne laisseroit pas d’estre» is ‘would not fail to be’: «ne pas laisser de» with an infinitive means ‘not to fail to’, that is, to do the thing all the same, and «laisseroit» is the conditional (modern «laisserait»). «estre» is «être» ‘to be’, with an s before the consonant where modern French has a circumflex. «aimable» is stronger than English ‘amiable’: ‘worthy of love, winning’. «esprit» is the word the tale turns on; see the next unit.

sentences.t: elle ajoûta même qu’il pourroit, en vertu du don qu’elle venoit de luy faire, donner autant d’esprit qu’il en auroit à la personne qu’il aimeroit le mieux.
sentences.say: elle ajouta même qu’il pourrait, en vertu du don qu’elle venait de lui faire, donner autant d’esprit qu’il en aurait à la personne qu’il aimerait le mieux.
sentences.l: she added even that he would be able, by virtue of the gift that she had just made him, to give as much wit as he would have of it to the person that he would love the best.
sentences.i: She even added that, by virtue of the gift she had just bestowed on him, he would be able to give as much wit as he had himself to the person he came to love best.
sentences.n: «esprit» here is ‘wit’, a quick and graceful mind, not ‘spirit’, and the whole tale turns on it. «venoit de luy faire» is ‘had just made him’ («venir de» with an infinitive is the French ‘to have just’), and «pourroit», «auroit», «aimeroit» are conditionals carrying the Fairy’s prophecy into the past. «en» in «qu’il en auroit» is ‘of it’: as much as he himself would have. «ajoûta» is the passé simple of «ajouter» ‘to add’, with a circumflex modern French has dropped, and «même» here is ‘even’. «luy» is «lui» ‘him’ with the 1697 y.

sentences.t: Tout cela consola un peu la pauvre Reine, qui estoit bien affligée d’avoir mis au monde un si vilain marmot.
sentences.say: Tout cela consola un peu la pauvre Reine, qui était bien affligée d’avoir mis au monde un si vilain marmot.
sentences.l: All that consoled a little the poor Queen, who was much afflicted at having put into the world so ugly a brat.
sentences.i: All this comforted the poor Queen a little, for she was sorely grieved to have brought so ugly a brat into the world.
sentences.n: «mettre au monde» ‘to put into the world’ is ‘to give birth to’. «bien affligée» is ‘deeply distressed’: «bien» before an adjective strengthens it. «vilain» is ‘ugly’, with an old undertone of ‘base, low’. «marmot» is a familiar word for a small child, with a note of mockery, and it also named a small monkey; ‘brat’ keeps some of its edge. «estoit» is «était» ‘was’.

sentences.t: Il est vray que cet enfant ne commença pas plutost à parler qu’il dit mille jolies choses, & qu’il avoit dans toutes ses actions je ne sçai quoi de si spirituel qu’on en estoit charmé.
sentences.say: Il est vrai que cet enfant ne commença pas plutôt à parler qu’il dit mille jolies choses, et qu’il avait dans toutes ses actions je ne sais quoi de si spirituel qu’on en était charmé.
sentences.l: It is true that this child did not begin sooner to speak than he said a thousand pretty things, and that he had in all his actions I know not what of so witty that one was charmed by it.
sentences.i: It is true that no sooner had the child begun to talk than he said a thousand charming things, and that there was a certain something so witty in all he did that everyone was enchanted.
sentences.n: «ne … pas plutost … que» ‘not sooner … than’ is ‘no sooner … than’; «plutost» is the 1697 spelling of «plus tôt» ‘sooner’. «vray» is «vrai» ‘true’, with the 1697 y, and «dit» is the passé simple ‘said’, spelt like the present. «je ne sçai quoi» ‘I know not what’ was the polite world’s phrase for a charm too fine to name. The «sç» of «sçai» (modern «sais») was added in the belief that the verb came from Latin «scire»; it comes from «sapere». «spirituel» is ‘witty’, the adjective of «esprit», and «charmé» is stronger than the English: ‘enchanted, delighted’, with a memory of «charme» ‘a spell’.

sentences.t: J’oubliois de dire qu’il vint au monde avec une petite houppe de cheveux sur la teste, ce qui fit qu’on le nomma Riquet à la houppe, car Riquet estoit le nom de la famille.
sentences.say: J’oubliais de dire qu’il vint au monde avec une petite houppe de cheveux sur la tête, ce qui fit qu’on le nomma Riquet à la houppe, car Riquet était le nom de la famille.
sentences.l: I was forgetting to say that he came into the world with a little tuft of hair on the head, which made that one named him Riquet with the Tuft, for Riquet was the name of the family.
sentences.i: I forgot to say that he was born with a little tuft of hair on his head, which is why he was called Riquet with the Tuft, Riquet being the family name.
sentences.n: «houppe» is a tuft of hair, and «à la houppe» ‘with the tuft’ turns it into a name, as French names a person by a distinguishing mark; the English is ‘Riquet with the Tuft’ in both lines throughout. The tale gives «Riquet» simply as the family name. «J’oubliois» (modern «j’oubliais») ‘I was forgetting’ is the narrator stepping into his own story. «teste» is «tête» ‘head’, and where French says ‘the head’ English says ‘his head’. «ce qui fit qu’on le nomma» ‘which made that one named him’ is ‘which is why he was named’; «vint», «fit» and «nomma» are passé simple.

sentences.t: Au bout de sept ou huit ans, la Reine d’un Royaume voisin accoucha de deux filles.
sentences.l: At the end of seven or eight years, the Queen of a neighbouring Kingdom gave birth to two daughters.
sentences.i: Some seven or eight years later, the Queen of a neighbouring kingdom gave birth to two daughters.
sentences.n: «Au bout de» ‘at the end of’ is ‘after’. «Royaume voisin» sets the adjective after the noun, as French usually does: ‘a kingdom neighbouring’. The two daughters are born moments apart, as the next units tell, so the sisters are twins. «accoucha de» ‘was delivered of’ is the passé simple again.

sentences.t: La premiere qui vint au monde estoit plus belle que le jour ;
sentences.say: La première qui vint au monde était plus belle que le jour ;
sentences.l: The first who came into the world was more beautiful than the day;
sentences.i: The first to be born was lovelier than the day;
sentences.n: «plus belle que le jour» ‘more beautiful than the day’ is a set phrase of praise, ‘as fair as daylight’, and the English keeps its image. «premiere» lacks the grave accent of modern «première».

sentences.t: la Reine en fut si aise qu’on apprehenda que la trop grande joye qu’elle en avoit ne luy fit mal.
sentences.say: la Reine en fut si aise qu’on appréhenda que la trop grande joie qu’elle en avait ne lui fit mal.
sentences.l: the Queen was so glad of it that one feared that the too great joy that she had of it might do her harm.
sentences.i: the Queen was so overjoyed that people feared her excess of joy might do her harm.
sentences.n: «en» ‘of it’, twice, points back to the birth. «aise» is ‘glad’, and «apprehenda» (modern «appréhenda») is ‘feared’: after a verb of fearing French sets a «ne» that adds no negation and puts the verb in the subjunctive. «fit» here stands for «fît», the imperfect subjunctive, printed without its circumflex: a formal tense, used after «que» when the main verb is past, which everyday French has given up; English says ‘might’ or uses a plain past. «faire mal à» is ‘to harm’, and «joye» is the 1697 spelling of «joie».

sentences.t: La même Fée qui avoit assisté à la naissance du petit Riquet à la Houppe estoit presente, & pour moderer la joye de la Reine, elle luy declara que cette petite Princesse n’auroit point d’esprit, & qu’elle seroit aussi stupide qu’elle estoit belle.
sentences.say: La même Fée qui avait assisté à la naissance du petit Riquet à la Houppe était présente, et pour modérer la joie de la Reine, elle lui déclara que cette petite Princesse n’aurait point d’esprit, et qu’elle serait aussi stupide qu’elle était belle.
sentences.l: The same fairy who had been present at the birth of little Riquet with the Tuft was present, and to moderate the joy of the Queen, she declared to her that this little Princess would have no wit at all, and that she would be as stupid as she was beautiful.
sentences.i: The same fairy who had attended the birth of little Riquet with the Tuft was there, and, to temper the Queen’s joy, she told her that this little princess would have no wit whatever, and would be as stupid as she was beautiful.
sentences.n: «assister à» is ‘to be present at, attend’, not ‘to assist’. «ne … point» is a firmer ‘not’ than «ne … pas»: ‘no wit at all’. The witness prints «Houppe» with a capital here and «houppe» elsewhere; it is the same name. «presente», «moderer» and «declara» lack the accents of modern «présente», «modérer», «déclara», and «auroit», «seroit» are «aurait», «serait».

sentences.t: Cela mortifia beaucoup la Reine ; mais elle eut, quelques momens aprés un bien plus grand chagrin, car la seconde fille dont elle accoucha, se trouva extremement laide.
sentences.say: Cela mortifia beaucoup la Reine ; mais elle eut, quelques moments après un bien plus grand chagrin, car la seconde fille dont elle accoucha, se trouva extrêmement laide.
sentences.l: That mortified much the Queen; but she had, some moments after a much greater sorrow, for the second daughter of whom she was delivered, turned out extremely ugly.
sentences.i: This was a bitter blow to the Queen; but a few moments later she had a far greater grief, for the second daughter she bore proved extremely ugly.
sentences.n: «mortifier» in 1697 is ‘to humble, to wound deeply’, a stronger word than it has become. «chagrin» is ‘grief, sorrow’, not merely ‘vexation’. «momens» is the old plural of «moment», written without its t, and «aprés» carries an acute accent where modern «après» has a grave; the comma one expects after it is not printed. «se trouva» ‘found itself’ is ‘turned out to be’, and «eut» ‘had’ is the passé simple of «avoir»; «extremement» is «extrêmement».

sentences.t: Ne vous affligez point tant Madame, luy dit la Fée ; vostre fille sera recompensée d’ailleurs, & elle aura tant d’esprit, qu’on ne s’apercevra presque pas qu’il luy manque de la beauté.
sentences.say: Ne vous affligez point tant Madame, lui dit la Fée ; votre fille sera récompensée d’ailleurs, et elle aura tant d’esprit, qu’on ne s’apercevra presque pas qu’il lui manque de la beauté.
sentences.l: Do not afflict yourself so much Madame, said to her the fairy; your daughter will be recompensed from elsewhere, and she will have so much wit, that one will almost not perceive that beauty is lacking to her.
sentences.i: Do not grieve so, Madame, the fairy said to her; your daughter will be recompensed in another way, and she will have so much wit that people will scarcely notice her want of beauty.
sentences.n: «Madame» is how the fairy addresses a queen, as anyone at court would, and the English keeps the French word; the comma before it is not printed. «s’affliger» ‘to afflict oneself’ is ‘to grieve’. «d’ailleurs» keeps its old sense ‘from elsewhere, in another way’. In «il luy manque de la beauté» ‘there lacks to her some beauty’ French makes the lack impersonal, where English says ‘she lacks’. «vostre» is «votre» and «recompensée» «récompensée».

sentences.t: Dieu le veüille, répondit la Reine ; mais n’y auroit-il point moyen de faire avoir un peu d’esprit à l’aînée, qui est si belle ?
sentences.say: Dieu le veuille, répondit la Reine ; mais n’y aurait-il point moyen de faire avoir un peu d’esprit à l’aînée, qui est si belle ?
sentences.l: May God will it, answered the Queen; but would there be no means of making the elder have a little wit, who is so beautiful?
sentences.i: May God grant it, replied the Queen; but is there no way to give a little wit to the elder, who is so beautiful?
sentences.n: «Dieu le veüille» ‘may God will it’ is a present subjunctive of wish, standing alone without «que»; «veüille» is the 1697 spelling of «veuille». «faire avoir» ‘to make have’ is ‘to cause someone to have’. «l’aînée» is ‘the elder’: the book spells the word three ways, «aînée», «aisnée» and «ainée», all one word. «auroit-il» is «aurait-il», and «ne … point» makes the question ‘is there no way at all?’.

sentences.t: Je ne puis rien pour elle, Madame, du costé de l’esprit, luy dit la Fée ; mais je puis tout du costé de la beauté ;
sentences.say: Je ne puis rien pour elle, Madame, du côté de l’esprit, lui dit la Fée ; mais je puis tout du côté de la beauté ;
sentences.l: I can do nothing for her, Madame, on the side of wit, said to her the fairy; but I can do everything on the side of beauty;
sentences.i: I can do nothing for her in the way of wit, Madame, said the fairy; but in the way of beauty I can do everything;
sentences.n: «je ne puis» is the older, still literary form of «je ne peux» ‘I cannot’, and «ne … rien» ‘nothing’ is answered by «tout» ‘everything’. «du costé de» ‘on the side of’ is ‘as regards’; «costé» is the 1697 spelling of «côté». «luy dit la Fée» puts the subject after the verb, as French does in a speech tag.

sentences.t: & comme il n’y a rien que je ne veüille faire pour vôtre satisfaction, je vais luy donner pour don de pouvoir rendre beau ou belle la personne qui luy plaira.
sentences.say: et comme il n’y a rien que je ne veuille faire pour vôtre satisfaction, je vais lui donner pour don de pouvoir rendre beau ou belle la personne qui lui plaira.
sentences.l: and as there is nothing that I would not wish to do for your satisfaction, I am going to give her as a gift to be able to make handsome or beautiful the person who will please her.
sentences.i: and since there is nothing I would not do to satisfy you, I shall give her the gift of being able to make whoever pleases her handsome or beautiful.
sentences.n: «rendre beau ou belle» ‘to make handsome or beautiful’ gives the adjective in both genders because the person may be a man or a woman, which the tale will need; English does the same work with two words. «qui luy plaira» is ‘who will please her’, that is, whoever she likes, and «je vais» with an infinitive is the near future, ‘I am going to’. In «rien que je ne veüille faire» ‘nothing that I would not wish to do’ the subjunctive «veüille» follows «rien que», and here the «ne» is a real negation. The witness spells the same word «vôtre» here and «vostre» a few lines before.

sentences.t: A mesure que ces deux Princesses devinrent grandes, leurs perfections crûrent aussi avec elles, & on ne parloit partout que de la beauté de l’aisnée, & de l’esprit de la cadette.
sentences.say: A mesure que ces deux Princesses devinrent grandes, leurs perfections crûrent aussi avec elles, et on ne parlait partout que de la beauté de l’aînée, et de l’esprit de la cadette.
sentences.l: In measure as these two Princesses became grown, their perfections grew also with them, and one spoke everywhere only of the beauty of the elder, and of the wit of the younger.
sentences.i: As the two princesses grew up, their perfections grew with them, and everywhere people talked of nothing but the beauty of the elder and the wit of the younger.
sentences.n: «A mesure que» (modern «à mesure que») is ‘in proportion as, as’; the printer sets the capital without its accent. «devinrent» and «crûrent» are passé simple, of «devenir» ‘to become’ and «croître» ‘to grow’. «ne … que» is ‘nothing but, only’. «la cadette» is ‘the younger (daughter)’, and «l’aisnée» ‘the elder’ has the 1697 s before the n.

sentences.t: Il est vray aussi que leurs défauts augmenterent beaucoup avec l’âge.
sentences.say: Il est vrai aussi que leurs défauts augmentèrent beaucoup avec l’âge.
sentences.l: It is true also that their defects increased much with age.
sentences.i: It is also true that their failings grew much worse as they grew older.
sentences.n: «défauts» are ‘defects, failings’, and «augmenterent» is the passé simple «augmentèrent» ‘increased’, printed without its grave accent. «vray» is «vrai», as in the first paragraph.

sentences.t: La cadette enlaidissoit à veuë d’œil, & l’ainée devenoit plus stupide de jour en jour.
sentences.say: La cadette enlaidissait à vue d’œil, et l’aînée devenait plus stupide de jour en jour.
sentences.l: The younger grew uglier at sight of eye, and the elder became more stupid from day to day.
sentences.i: The younger grew visibly uglier, and the elder more stupid day by day.
sentences.n: «à veuë d’œil» ‘at sight of eye’ is ‘visibly, before one’s eyes’; «veuë» is the 1697 spelling of «vue». «enlaidissoit» (modern «enlaidissait») ‘grew ugly’ is built on «laid» ‘ugly’, and it and «devenoit» are imperfects, a change still going on. «ainée» is the third of the book’s spellings of «aînée».

sentences.t: Ou elle ne répondoit rien à ce qu’on lui demandoit, ou elle disoit une sottise.
sentences.say: Ou elle ne répondait rien à ce qu’on lui demandait, ou elle disait une sottise.
sentences.l: Either she answered nothing to what one asked her, or she said a foolishness.
sentences.i: Either she made no answer to what she was asked, or she said something foolish.
sentences.n: «Ou … ou» is ‘either … or’. The imperfects «répondoit», «demandoit», «disoit» (modern «répondait», «demandait», «disait») tell what happened time after time. A «sottise» is ‘a foolish remark’, from «sot» ‘fool’. The book prints «lui» here and «luy» elsewhere: the same word.

sentences.t: Elle estoit avec cela si maladroite qu’elle n’eust pû ranger quatre porcelaines sur le bord d’une cheminée sans en casser une, ny boire un verre d’eau sans en répandre la moitié sur ses habits.
sentences.say: Elle était avec cela si maladroite qu’elle n’eût pu ranger quatre porcelaines sur le bord d’une cheminée sans en casser une, ni boire un verre d’eau sans en répandre la moitié sur ses habits.
sentences.l: She was with that so clumsy that she could not have arranged four porcelains on the edge of a chimney-piece without breaking one of them, nor drunk a glass of water without spilling half of it on her clothes.
sentences.i: Besides this she was so clumsy that she could not have set out four pieces of china along a mantelpiece without breaking one, nor drunk a glass of water without spilling half of it down her dress.
sentences.n: «avec cela» ‘with that’ is ‘besides’. «n’eust pû» (modern «n’eût pu») ‘could not have’ is the pluperfect subjunctive standing, as literary French still lets it, for the past conditional. Pieces of porcelain from China set out along the mantelpiece were a fashion of grand rooms in Perrault’s day, and «le bord d’une cheminée» is the shelf above the fireplace. «ny» is «ni» ‘nor’, «en» is ‘of them’ and ‘of it’, and «habits» are ‘clothes’.

sentences.t: Quoy que la beauté soit un grand avantage dans une jeune personne, cependant la cadette l’emportoit presque toûjours sur son aînée dans toutes les Compagnies.
sentences.say: Quoi que la beauté soit un grand avantage dans une jeune personne, cependant la cadette l’emportait presque toujours sur son aînée dans toutes les Compagnies.
sentences.l: Although beauty be a great advantage in a young person, nevertheless the younger carried it almost always over her elder in all the Companies.
sentences.i: Great as the advantage of beauty is in a young woman, the younger sister nearly always outshone the elder in every gathering.
sentences.n: «Quoy que» (modern «quoique») ‘although’ takes the subjunctive «soit». «cependant» is ‘nevertheless’, restating the concession, a habit of the French of the time. «l’emporter sur» ‘to carry it over’ is ‘to prevail over, outshine’. «Compagnies» are social gatherings, the company assembled in a drawing room. «toûjours» is «toujours» ‘always’, with a circumflex modern French has dropped.

sentences.t: D’abord on alloit du costé de la plus belle, pour la voir & pour l’admirer, mais bien tost aprés, on alloit à celle qui avoit le plus d’esprit pour luy entendre dire mille choses agreables ;
sentences.say: D’abord on allait du côté de la plus belle, pour la voir et pour l’admirer, mais bien tôt après, on allait à celle qui avait le plus d’esprit pour lui entendre dire mille choses agréables ;
sentences.l: At first one went towards the side of the more beautiful, to see her and to admire her, but very soon after, one went to the one who had the more wit to hear her say a thousand agreeable things;
sentences.i: At first people would go over to the more beautiful one, to look at her and admire her, but very soon afterwards they would go to the one with more wit, to hear her say a thousand delightful things;
sentences.n: «on alloit» (modern «on allait») ‘one went’ is the imperfect of habit: this happened at gathering after gathering. «bien tost» is «bientôt» ‘soon’, printed as two words. «luy entendre dire» ‘to her to hear say’ is ‘to hear her say’, with the pronoun before «entendre». «le plus» is ‘the most’, which between two sisters English makes ‘the more’. «agreables» lacks the accent of «agréables».

sentences.t: & on estoit estonné qu’en moins d’un quart d’heure l’aînée n’avoit plus personne auprés d’elle, & que tout le monde s’estoit rangé autour de la cadette.
sentences.say: et on était étonné qu’en moins d’un quart d’heure l’aînée n’avait plus personne auprès d’elle, et que tout le monde s’était rangé autour de la cadette.
sentences.l: and one was astonished that in less than a quarter of an hour the elder no longer had anyone near her, and that all the world had ranged itself around the younger.
sentences.i: and it was astonishing to see how, in less than a quarter of an hour, the elder was left with no one beside her, while everyone had gathered round the younger.
sentences.n: «estonné» is «étonné» ‘astonished’, and «tout le monde» ‘all the world’ is ‘everyone’. «ne … plus personne» is ‘no longer anyone’. «s’estoit rangé» ‘had ranged itself’ is ‘had gathered, taken its place’. «auprés» is «auprès» ‘near, beside’.

sentences.t: L’aisnée quoy que fort stupide, le remarqua bien, & elle eut donné sans regret toute sa beauté pour avoir la moitié de l’esprit de sa sœur.
sentences.say: L’aînée quoi que fort stupide, le remarqua bien, et elle eut donné sans regret toute sa beauté pour avoir la moitié de l’esprit de sa sœur.
sentences.l: The elder although very stupid, noticed it well, and she would have given without regret all her beauty to have half of the wit of her sister.
sentences.i: The elder, stupid as she was, noticed it well enough, and she would gladly have given all her beauty for half her sister’s wit.
sentences.n: «fort» ‘strongly’ is ‘very’, and «remarqua» is passé simple. «eut donné» ‘would have given’ stands for «eût donné», the pluperfect subjunctive with the force of a past conditional, printed without its circumflex; as it is printed it looks like the past anterior ‘had given’, which the sense does not allow. «sœur» ‘sister’ is printed with the joined œ.

sentences.t: La Reine toute sage qu’elle estoit, ne put s’empêcher de luy reprocher plusieurs fois sa bestise, ce qui pensa faire mourir de douleur cette pauvre Princesse.
sentences.say: La Reine toute sage qu’elle était, ne put s’empêcher de lui reprocher plusieurs fois sa bêtise, ce qui pensa faire mourir de douleur cette pauvre Princesse.
sentences.l: The Queen all wise that she was, could not keep herself from reproaching her several times with her stupidity, which nearly made this poor Princess die of grief.
sentences.i: Wise as she was, the Queen could not help reproaching her more than once for her stupidity, and it nearly made the poor princess die of grief.
sentences.n: «toute sage qu’elle estoit» ‘all wise that she was’ is ‘wise as she was’. «s’empêcher de» is ‘to keep oneself from, help’. «pensa faire mourir» ‘thought to make die’: «penser» with an infinitive meant ‘to come near to, all but’, a use now gone. «bestise» is the 1697 spelling of «bêtise» ‘stupidity’, built on «bête» ‘beast’.

sentences.t: Un jour qu’elle s’estoit retirée dans un bois pour y plaindre son malheur, elle vit venir à elle un petit homme fort laid & fort desagreable, mais vestu tres-magnifiquement.
sentences.say: Un jour qu’elle s’était retirée dans un bois pour y plaindre son malheur, elle vit venir à elle un petit homme fort laid et fort désagréable, mais vêtu très-magnifiquement.
sentences.l: One day that she had withdrawn into a wood in order there to lament her misfortune, she saw come to her a little man very ugly and very disagreeable, but dressed very magnificently.
sentences.i: One day, when she had gone off into a wood to bewail her misfortune, she saw coming towards her a little man, very ugly and most unpleasing, but very magnificently dressed.
sentences.n: «Un jour que» ‘one day that’ is ‘one day when’. «y» ‘there’ points back to the wood, and «plaindre son malheur» is ‘to lament her misfortune’. «voir venir» is ‘to see coming’. «desagreable» (modern «désagréable») is ‘disagreeable, displeasing’, set beside «laid» ‘ugly’ as a second fault. «vestu» is «vêtu» ‘dressed’, and «tres-magnifiquement» joins «très» ‘very’ to its word with a hyphen, as the book does.

sentences.t: C’estoit le jeune Prince Riquet à la houppe, qui estant devenu amoureux d’elle sur ses Portraits qui courroient par tout le monde, avoit quitté le Royaume de son pere pour avoir le plaisir de la voir & de luy parler.
sentences.say: C’était le jeune Prince Riquet à la houppe, qui étant devenu amoureux d’elle sur ses Portraits qui couraient par tout le monde, avait quitté le Royaume de son père pour avoir le plaisir de la voir et de lui parler.
sentences.l: It was the young Prince Riquet with the Tuft, who having become in love with her from her Portraits which ran through all the world, had left the Kingdom of his father to have the pleasure of seeing her and of speaking to her.
sentences.i: It was the young Prince Riquet with the Tuft, who had fallen in love with her from the portraits of her that went all over the world, and had left his father’s kingdom for the pleasure of seeing her and speaking with her.
sentences.n: «estant» is «étant» ‘being’, and «devenir amoureux de» ‘to become in love with’ is ‘to fall in love with’. Portraits of princesses of marriageable age were painted and sent to other courts, and a prince might lose his heart to a likeness before he ever saw the sitter. «courroient» (modern «couraient») ‘ran’ is ‘circulated’. «pere» lacks the accent of «père».

sentences.t: Ravi de la rencontrer ainsi toute seule, il l’aborde avec tout le respect & toute la politesse imaginable.
sentences.say: Ravi de la rencontrer ainsi toute seule, il l’aborde avec tout le respect et toute la politesse imaginable.
sentences.l: Delighted to meet her thus all alone, he approaches her with all the respect and all the politeness imaginable.
sentences.i: Delighted to find her quite alone, he approached her with all the respect and courtesy imaginable.
sentences.n: «aborder» is ‘to approach and speak to’ someone. The witness prints the present «aborde» among past tenses: it may be a vivid narrative present or a slip for the passé simple «aborda», and the sense is the same either way; the literal line keeps the present, the idiomatic line uses the past, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «imaginable» agrees with the nearer noun, «politesse».

sentences.t: Ayant remarqué aprés luy avoir fait les complimens ordinaires, qu’elle estoit fort melancolique, il luy dit ; je ne comprens point, Madame, comment une personne aussi belle que vous l’estes, peut estre aussi triste que vous le paraissiez ;
sentences.say: Ayant remarqué après lui avoir fait les compliments ordinaires, qu’elle était fort mélancolique, il lui dit ; je ne comprends point, Madame, comment une personne aussi belle que vous l’êtes, peut être aussi triste que vous le paraissiez ;
sentences.l: Having noticed after having made her the ordinary compliments, that she was very melancholy, he said to her; I do not understand at all, Madame, how a person as beautiful as you are, can be as sad as you appeared;
sentences.i: Having observed, after paying her the customary compliments, that she was very melancholy, he said to her: I cannot understand, Madame, how anyone as beautiful as you are can be as sad as you seem;
sentences.n: «les complimens ordinaires» are the customary civilities of a greeting; «complimens» drops the t of the plural, like «momens». «melancolique» (modern «mélancolique») is ‘melancholy, low in spirits’. In «que vous l’estes» and «que vous le paraissiez» the «le» stands for the adjective, ‘as you are (so)’, which English leaves out. The witness prints the modern spelling «paraissiez» where the book elsewhere writes «paroissoit»; both are the verb «paraître» ‘to seem’. «comprens» is «comprends», and «il luy dit ;» has a semicolon where modern French puts a colon before speech.

sentences.t: car quoy que je puisse me vanter d’avoir veu une infinité de belles personnes, je puis dire que je n’en ay jamais vû dont la beauté approche de la vostre.
sentences.say: car quoi que je puisse me vanter d’avoir vu une infinité de belles personnes, je puis dire que je n’en ai jamais vu dont la beauté approche de la votre.
sentences.l: for although I may boast of having seen an infinity of beautiful persons, I can say that I have never seen one of them whose beauty approaches yours.
sentences.i: for though I may boast of having seen a vast number of beauties, I can say I have never seen one whose beauty comes near yours.
sentences.n: «puisse» is the subjunctive after «quoy que» ‘although’. The book spells the participle of «voir» both «veu» and «vû» in one sentence (modern «vu»). In «je n’en ay jamais vû» ‘I have never seen any of them’ «en» is ‘of them’, and «ay» is «ai» ‘have’. «une infinité» ‘an infinity’ is a courtier’s ‘a countless number’.

sentences.t: Cela vous plaist à dire, Monsieur, lui répondit la Princesse, & en demeura là.
sentences.say: Cela vous plaît à dire, Monsieur, lui répondit la Princesse, et en demeura là.
sentences.l: That pleases you to say, Monsieur, answered him the Princess, and remained at that.
sentences.i: You are pleased to say so, Monsieur, the Princess replied, and said no more.
sentences.n: «Cela vous plaist à dire» ‘that pleases you to say’ was a polite formula for turning a compliment aside: ‘you are pleased to say so’. «plaist» is the 1697 spelling of «plaît». «en demeurer là» ‘to remain there’ is ‘to go no further, leave it at that’. «Monsieur» is the courteous address to a gentleman, and the English keeps it as it keeps «Madame».

sentences.t: La beauté, reprit Riquet à la houppe, est un si grand avantage qu’il doit tenir lieu de tout le reste ; & quand on le possede, je ne voy pas qu’il y ait rien qui puisse nous affliger beaucoup.
sentences.say: La beauté, reprit Riquet à la houppe, est un si grand avantage qu’il doit tenir lieu de tout le reste ; et quand on le possède, je ne vois pas qu’il y ait rien qui puisse nous affliger beaucoup.
sentences.l: Beauty, resumed Riquet with the Tuft, is so great an advantage that it must hold the place of all the rest; and when one possesses it, I do not see that there may be anything that can afflict us much.
sentences.i: Beauty, Riquet with the Tuft went on, is so great an advantage that it must stand in place of everything else; and when one has it, I do not see that anything can trouble us very much.
sentences.n: «reprit», the passé simple of «reprendre» ‘to take up again’, is a speech tag for ‘went on, rejoined’. «tenir lieu de» ‘to hold the place of’ is ‘to make up for, stand in for’. «il» and «le» stand for «avantage», which is masculine. «je ne voy pas qu’il y ait» ‘I do not see that there be’ takes the subjunctive after a denied verb of seeing; «voy» is «vois», and «possede» is «possède».

sentences.t: J’aimerois mieux, dit la Princesse, estre aussi laide que vous & avoir de l’esprit, que d’avoir de la beauté comme j’en ay, & estre beste autant que je le suis.
sentences.say: J’aimerais mieux, dit la Princesse, être aussi laide que vous et avoir de l’esprit, que d’avoir de la beauté comme j’en ai, et être bête autant que je le suis.
sentences.l: I would like better, said the Princess, to be as ugly as you and to have wit, than to have beauty as I have it, and to be stupid as much as I am.
sentences.i: I would rather, said the Princess, be as ugly as you and have wit, than have beauty such as mine and be as stupid as I am.
sentences.n: «aimer mieux» ‘to like better’ is ‘to prefer, would rather’, and «aimerois» is the conditional (modern «aimerais»). «beste» is «bête», here an adjective, ‘stupid’, literally ‘beastlike’. «de l’esprit» and «de la beauté» are partitives, ‘some wit, some beauty’, and in «comme j’en ay» ‘as I have of it’ «en» picks up the beauty. In «que je le suis» the «le» again stands for the adjective.

sentences.t: Il n’y a rien, Madame, qui marque d’avantage qu’on a de l’esprit que de croire n’en pas avoir, & il est de la nature de ce bien-là, que plus on en a, plus on croit en manquer.
sentences.say: Il n’y a rien, Madame, qui marque d’avantage qu’on a de l’esprit que de croire n’en pas avoir, et il est de la nature de ce bien-là, que plus on en a, plus on croit en manquer.
sentences.l: There is nothing, Madame, that shows more that one has wit than to believe one has none, and it is in the nature of that good, that the more one has of it, the more one believes one lacks it.
sentences.i: Nothing shows more plainly that one has wit, Madame, than to believe one has none; and it is in the nature of that blessing that the more of it one has, the more one feels the want of it.
sentences.n: «d’avantage» is the older spelling of «davantage» ‘more’. «croire n’en pas avoir» ‘to believe not to have any’ sets «ne pas» together before the infinitive. «plus … plus» is ‘the more … the more’. «bien» here is a noun, ‘a good, a possession’, and «ce bien-là» ‘that good’. Riquet’s compliment is also a maxim, turned in the manner of polite conversation of the day.

sentences.t: Je ne sçay pas cela, dit la Princesse, mais je sçay bien que je suis fort beste, & c’est de là que vient le chagrin qui me tuë.
sentences.say: Je ne sais pas cela, dit la Princesse, mais je sais bien que je suis fort bête, et c’est de là que vient le chagrin qui me tue.
sentences.l: I do not know that, said the Princess, but I know well that I am very stupid, and it is from there that comes the grief that is killing me.
sentences.i: I know nothing of that, said the Princess, but I know very well that I am exceedingly stupid, and that is the source of the grief that is killing me.
sentences.n: «sçay» is «sais» ‘know’, with the 1697 «sç» and y. «c’est de là que vient» ‘it is from there that comes’ puts the weight on «de là» ‘from there’ and the subject after the verb. «tuë» is «tue» ‘kills’, with a diaeresis the printer puts on a final e after u (as in «veuë»), which modern French does not. «chagrin» is again ‘grief’.

sentences.t: Si ce n’est que cela, Madame, qui vous afflige, je puis aisement mettre fin à vostre douleur.
sentences.say: Si ce n’est que cela, Madame, qui vous afflige, je puis aisément mettre fin à votre douleur.
sentences.l: If it is only that, Madame, which afflicts you, I can easily put an end to your sorrow.
sentences.i: If that is all that troubles you, Madame, I can easily put an end to your sorrow.
sentences.n: «Si ce n’est que cela … qui» ‘if it is only that … which’ is ‘if that is all that’. «aisement» is «aisément» ‘easily’, and «douleur» is ‘pain, sorrow’, of the mind as well as the body.

sentences.t: Et comment ferez-vous, dit la Princesse ?
sentences.l: And how will you do, said the Princess?
sentences.i: And how will you do that? said the Princess.
sentences.n: «faire» ‘to do’ stands alone, like English ‘how will you manage?’. The printer puts the question mark after the speech tag, at the end of the sentence, not after the words spoken, and «ferez-vous» sets the subject after the verb, as a question does.

sentences.t: J’ay le pouvoir, Madame, dit Riquet à la houppe, de donner de l’esprit autant qu’on en sçauroit avoir à la personne que je dois aimer le plus ; & comme vous estes, Madame, cette personne, il ne tiendra qu’à vous que vous n’ayez autant d’esprit qu’on en peut avoir, pourvû que vous vouliez bien m’épouser.
sentences.say: J’ai le pouvoir, Madame, dit Riquet à la houppe, de donner de l’esprit autant qu’on en saurait avoir à la personne que je dois aimer le plus ; et comme vous êtes, Madame, cette personne, il ne tiendra qu’à vous que vous n’ayez autant d’esprit qu’on en peut avoir, pourvu que vous vouliez bien m’épouser.
sentences.l: I have the power, Madame, said Riquet with the Tuft, to give wit, as much as one could have of it, to the person whom I am to love the most; and as you are, Madame, that person, it will rest only with you that you have as much wit as one can have of it, provided that you are willing to marry me.
sentences.i: I have the power, Madame, said Riquet with the Tuft, to give as much wit as anyone could possess to the person I am destined to love most; and since you, Madame, are that person, it rests with you alone to have all the wit a person can have, provided you are willing to marry me.
sentences.n: «il ne tiendra qu’à vous que vous n’ayez» is ‘it will rest only with you that you have’: «il ne tient qu’à» is ‘it depends only on’, and the «ne» before the subjunctive «ayez» adds no negation, as often after such phrases. «que je dois aimer le plus» is ‘whom I am to love most’, with «devoir» marking what is destined, and «pourvû que» ‘provided that’ takes the subjunctive «vouliez». «J’ay» is «j’ai», «sçauroit» «saurait», «estes» «êtes» and «pourvû» «pourvu», all 1697 spellings.

sentences.t: La Princesse demeura toute interdite, & ne répondit rien.
sentences.say: La Princesse demeura toute interdite, et ne répondit rien.
sentences.l: The Princess remained all disconcerted, and answered nothing.
sentences.i: The Princess was quite taken aback, and made no reply.
sentences.n: «interdit» is ‘dumbfounded, at a loss for words’, not the modern ‘forbidden’, and «toute» ‘quite’ agrees with the Princess. «demeura» ‘remained’ and «répondit» are passé simple.

sentences.t: Je voy, reprit Riquet à la houppe, que cette proposition vous fait de la peine, & je ne m’en estonne pas ; mais je vous donne un an tout entier pour vous y resoudre.
sentences.say: Je vois, reprit Riquet à la houppe, que cette proposition vous fait de la peine, et je ne m’en étonne pas ; mais je vous donne un an tout entier pour vous y résoudre.
sentences.l: I see, resumed Riquet with the Tuft, that this proposal gives you pain, and I am not astonished at it; but I give you a year all entire to resolve yourself to it.
sentences.i: I see, Riquet with the Tuft went on, that this proposal distresses you, and I do not wonder at it; but I give you a whole year to make up your mind to it.
sentences.n: «faire de la peine à» is ‘to distress, pain’. «s’estonner de» (modern «s’étonner») is ‘to wonder at’. «se resoudre à» (modern «se résoudre») ‘to resolve oneself to’ is ‘to bring oneself to’, and «y» ‘to it’ is the marriage. «un an tout entier» ‘a year all entire’ is ‘a whole year’.

sentences.t: La Princesse avoit si peu d’esprit, & en mesme temps une si grande envie d’en avoir, qu’elle s’imagina que la fin de cette année ne viendroit jamais ; de sorte qu’elle accepta la proposition qui luy estoit faite.
sentences.say: La Princesse avait si peu d’esprit, et en même temps une si grande envie d’en avoir, qu’elle s’imagina que la fin de cette année ne viendrait jamais ; de sorte qu’elle accepta la proposition qui lui était faite.
sentences.l: The Princess had so little wit, and at the same time so great a desire to have some, that she imagined that the end of this year would never come; so that she accepted the proposal which was made to her.
sentences.i: The Princess had so little wit, and at the same time so great a longing for it, that she imagined the end of the year would never come; and so she accepted the proposal made to her.
sentences.n: «mesme» is «même» ‘same’, spelt here with the 1697 s, though the book as often prints «même». «avoir envie de» is ‘to desire, long for’. «viendroit» (modern «viendrait») ‘would come’ is the future as seen from the past. «de sorte que» is ‘so that, with the result that’.

sentences.t: Elle n’eut pas plûtost promis à Riquet à la houppe, qu’elle l’épouseroit dans un an à pareil jour, qu’elle se sentit tout autre qu’elle n’estoit auparavant ;
sentences.say: Elle n’eut pas plutôt promis à Riquet à la houppe, qu’elle l’épouserait dans un an à pareil jour, qu’elle se sentit tout autre qu’elle n’était auparavant ;
sentences.l: She had not sooner promised Riquet with the Tuft, that she would marry him in a year on a like day, than she felt herself quite other than she was before;
sentences.i: No sooner had she promised Riquet with the Tuft that she would marry him a year from that very day than she felt herself quite different from what she had been before;
sentences.n: «n’eut pas plûtost promis … que» ‘had not sooner promised … than’ is ‘no sooner had she promised … than’, the pattern already met with the infant Riquet; «plûtost» is another spelling of «plutost», and «eut promis» is the past anterior. «à pareil jour» ‘on a like day’ is ‘on the same day of the year’. After «autre que» the «ne» of «n’estoit» adds no negation, and «épouseroit» is «épouserait».

sentences.t: elle se trouva une facilité incroyable à dire tout ce qui luy plaisoit, & à le dire d’une maniere fine, aisée & naturelle :
sentences.say: elle se trouva une facilité incroyable à dire tout ce qui lui plaisait, et à le dire d’une manière fine, aisée et naturelle :
sentences.l: she found herself an incredible ease in saying all that pleased her, and in saying it in a manner fine, easy and natural:
sentences.i: she found she could say whatever she pleased with incredible ease, and say it in a manner delicate, unforced and natural;
sentences.n: «se trouver une facilité» ‘to find oneself an ease’ is ‘to find one has a gift’. «tout ce qui luy plaisoit» ‘all that pleased her’ is ‘whatever she liked’, the verb «plaire» again. «fine» is ‘delicate, subtle’ and «aisée» ‘easy, unforced’: the qualities most admired in the conversation of polite society. «maniere» and «plaisoit» are «manière» and «plaisait».

sentences.t: elle commença dés ce moment une conversation galante, & soutenuë avec Riquet à la houppe, où elle brilla d’une telle force que Riquet à la houppe crut luy avoir donné plus d’esprit qu’il ne s’en estoit réservé pour luy même.
sentences.say: elle commença dès ce moment une conversation galante, et soutenue avec Riquet à la houppe, où elle brilla d’une telle force que Riquet à la houppe crut lui avoir donné plus d’esprit qu’il ne s’en était réservé pour lui même.
sentences.l: she began from that moment a conversation gallant, and sustained with Riquet with the Tuft, in which she shone with such force that Riquet with the Tuft believed he had given her more wit than he had kept of it for himself.
sentences.i: from that moment she began a polished and sustained conversation with Riquet with the Tuft, in which she shone so brilliantly that Riquet with the Tuft believed he had given her more wit than he had kept for himself.
sentences.n: «galant» has shifted: a «conversation galante» in 1697 is polished, witty, courteous talk, with a touch of attentiveness to a lady, of the kind prized in fashionable company; it is not ‘brave’ and not necessarily amorous. «soutenuë» (modern «soutenue») is ‘sustained, kept up’, and «dés» is «dès» ‘from’. «brilla» and «crut» are passé simple. In «qu’il ne s’en estoit réservé» ‘than he had reserved of it for himself’ the «ne» after «plus … que» adds no negation; «luy même» is modern «lui-même».

sentences.t: Quand elle fut retournée au palais, toute la Cour ne sçavoit que penser d’un changement si subit & si extraordinaire :
sentences.say: Quand elle fut retournée au palais, toute la Cour ne savait que penser d’un changement si subit et si extraordinaire :
sentences.l: When she had returned to the palace, all the Court did not know what to think of a change so sudden and so extraordinary:
sentences.i: When she had returned to the palace, the whole Court did not know what to make of so sudden and extraordinary a change;
sentences.n: «fut retournée» is the past anterior of «retourner», formed with «être». In «ne sçavoit que penser» ‘did not know what to think’ «savoir» does without «pas», and «que» is ‘what’. «la Cour» is the royal court, the nobles and officers who lived about the King.

sentences.t: car autant qu’on luy avoit oüy dire d’impertinences auparavant, autant luy entendoit-on dire des choses bien sensées & infiniment spirituelles.
sentences.say: car autant qu’on lui avait oui dire d’impertinences auparavant, autant lui entendait-on dire des choses bien sensées et infiniment spirituelles.
sentences.l: for as many as one had heard her say of absurdities before, so many did one hear her say things very sensible and infinitely witty.
sentences.i: for as many foolish things as they had heard her say before, just as many sensible and exceedingly witty things did they now hear from her.
sentences.n: «autant … autant» ‘as much … so much’ balances the before against the after. «impertinences» in 1697 are ‘absurdities, things said out of place’, not ‘insolent remarks’. «oüy» is the participle of «ouïr» ‘to hear’, a verb now nearly gone, and «entendoit-on» (modern «entendait-on») sets the subject after the verb, as French does after «autant» at the head of a clause. «bien sensées» is ‘very sensible’.

sentences.t: Toute la Cour en eut une joye qui ne se peut imaginer ;
sentences.say: Toute la Cour en eut une joie qui ne se peut imaginer ;
sentences.l: All the Court had of it a joy that cannot be imagined;
sentences.i: The whole Court was more delighted than can be imagined;
sentences.n: «qui ne se peut imaginer» ‘which cannot imagine itself’ is the reflexive standing for a passive, ‘which cannot be imagined’, with the pronoun before «peut», the 1697 order, where modern French says «ne peut s’imaginer». «en» ‘of it’ is the change.

sentences.t: il n’y eut que sa cadette qui n’en fut pas bien aise, parce que n’ayant plus sur son aisnée l’avantage de l’esprit, elle ne paroissoit plus auprés d’elle qu’une Guenon fort desagreable.
sentences.say: il n’y eut que sa cadette qui n’en fut pas bien aise, parce que n’ayant plus sur son aînée l’avantage de l’esprit, elle ne paraissait plus auprès d’elle qu’une Guenon fort désagréable.
sentences.l: there was only her younger sister who was not very glad of it, because not having any longer over her elder the advantage of wit, she no longer appeared beside her but a very disagreeable She-monkey.
sentences.i: only her younger sister was not pleased, because, no longer having the advantage of wit over the elder, she now looked like nothing but a most unpleasing she-monkey beside her.
sentences.n: «il n’y eut que … qui» ‘there was only … who’ is ‘only … was’. A «Guenon» is a female monkey, a byword for ugliness; the capital is the printer’s. «ne … plus … que» is ‘no longer anything but’. «paroissoit» is «paraissait» ‘appeared, looked’, and «fut» here is the passé simple ‘was’.

sentences.t: Le Roi se conduisoit par ses avis, & alloit même quelquefois tenir le Conseil dans son Appartement.
sentences.say: Le Roi se conduisait par ses avis, et allait même quelquefois tenir le Conseil dans son Appartement.
sentences.l: The King guided himself by her opinions, and went even sometimes to hold the Council in her Apartment.
sentences.i: The King was guided by her advice, and sometimes even went to hold his Council in her apartments.
sentences.n: The King’s «Conseil» was the council of ministers through whom he governed; to hold it in his daughter’s rooms was to give her a place in affairs of state. An «Appartement» at court was the suite of rooms belonging to one member of the royal family. «ses» and «son» can mean ‘his’ or ‘her’; the sense makes them the Princess’s. «conduisoit» is «conduisait», and «Roi» is printed here in its modern spelling, elsewhere «Roy».

sentences.t: Le bruit de ce changement s’estant répandu, tous les jeunes Princes des Royaumes voisins firent leurs efforts pour s’en faire aimer, & presque tous la demanderent en mariage ;
sentences.say: Le bruit de ce changement s’étant répandu, tous les jeunes Princes des Royaumes voisins firent leurs efforts pour s’en faire aimer, et presque tous la demandèrent en mariage ;
sentences.l: The noise of this change having spread, all the young Princes of the neighbouring Kingdoms made their efforts to make themselves loved by her, and almost all asked for her in marriage;
sentences.i: When word of the change had spread, all the young princes of the neighbouring kingdoms did their utmost to win her love, and nearly all of them asked for her hand;
sentences.n: «le bruit» ‘the noise’ is ‘the report, the rumour’, and «s’estant répandu» ‘having spread itself’ is an absolute construction: ‘the report having spread’. In «s’en faire aimer» ‘to make themselves loved by her’ «en» stands for the Princess. «demander en mariage» is ‘to ask for in marriage’, and «demanderent» is the passé simple «demandèrent».

sentences.t: mais elle n’en trouvoit point qui eust assez d’esprit, & elle les écoutoit tous, sans s’engager à pas un d’eux,
sentences.say: mais elle n’en trouvait point qui eût assez d’esprit, et elle les écoutait tous, sans s’engager à pas un d’eux,
sentences.l: but she did not find any of them who had enough wit, and she listened to them all, without binding herself to a single one of them,
sentences.i: but she found none of them with wit enough, and she listened to them all without committing herself to any.
sentences.n: «eust» (modern «eût») is the imperfect subjunctive, after «point … qui»: none who might have enough. «pas un» is ‘not one’, and «s’engager à» ‘to bind oneself to’. The witness ends this clause with a comma and begins the next word with a capital, where the sense wants a full stop; the English puts one, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Cependant il en vint un si puissant, si riche, si spirituel & si bien fait, qu’elle ne pust s’empêcher d’avoir de la bonne volonté pour luy.
sentences.say: Cependant il en vint un si puissant, si riche, si spirituel et si bien fait, qu’elle ne pût s’empêcher d’avoir de la bonne volonté pour lui.
sentences.l: Meanwhile there came of them one so powerful, so rich, so witty and so well made, that she could not keep herself from having good will for him.
sentences.i: Meanwhile one came who was so powerful, so rich, so witty and so handsome that she could not help feeling kindly towards him.
sentences.n: «Cependant» in 1697 is often ‘meanwhile’ as well as ‘however’, and either reading serves here. «il en vint un» ‘there came of them one’ is impersonal, with «en» ‘of them’, the princes. «bien fait» ‘well made’ is ‘handsome, well built’, the opposite of the «mal fait» of Riquet’s birth. «pust» is a 1697 spelling of «put» ‘could’, the passé simple of «pouvoir», which the tale earlier prints «put». «avoir de la bonne volonté pour» is ‘to feel kindly towards’.

sentences.t: Son pere s’en estant apperçû, luy dit qu’il la faisoit la maistresse sur le choix d’un Epoux, & qu’elle n’avoit qu’à se déclarer.
sentences.say: Son père s’en étant aperçu, lui dit qu’il la faisait la maîtresse sur le choix d’un Époux, et qu’elle n’avait qu’à se déclarer.
sentences.l: Her father having perceived it, told her that he made her the mistress over the choice of a Husband, and that she had only to declare herself.
sentences.i: Her father, noticing this, told her that he left the choice of a husband entirely to her, and that she had only to make her wishes known.
sentences.n: «s’apercevoir de» is ‘to notice’; «apperçû» is the 1697 spelling of «aperçu», with a double p. To make someone «maistresse» (modern «maîtresse») ‘mistress’ over a matter is to leave it wholly in her hands. «n’avoir qu’à» is ‘to have only to’, and «se déclarer» is ‘to declare oneself, say whom one chooses’.

sentences.t: Comme plus on a d’esprit & plus on a de peine à prendre une ferme resolution sur cette affaire, elle demanda, aprés avoir remercié son pere, qu’il luy donnast du temps pour y penser.
sentences.say: Comme plus on a d’esprit et plus on a de peine à prendre une ferme résolution sur cette affaire, elle demanda, après avoir remercié son père, qu’il lui donnât du temps pour y penser.
sentences.l: As the more one has wit the more one has trouble in taking a firm resolution on this matter, she asked, after having thanked her father, that he give her time to think of it.
sentences.i: Since the more wit one has, the harder one finds it to come to a firm decision in such a matter, she asked her father, after thanking him, to give her time to think it over.
sentences.n: «plus … & plus» ‘the more … and the more’ is an older form of «plus … plus» ‘the more … the more’; the literal line leaves out the ‘and’. «avoir de la peine à» is ‘to find it hard to’. «donnast» (modern «donnât») is the imperfect subjunctive, after «demanda que» ‘asked that’. «cette affaire» is marriage: the narrator smiles at the thought that wit makes choosing harder.

sentences.t: Elle alla par hasard se promener dans le même bois où elle avoit trouvé Riquet à la houppe, pour rêver plus commodement à ce qu’elle avoit à faire.
sentences.say: Elle alla par hasard se promener dans le même bois où elle avait trouvé Riquet à la houppe, pour rêver plus commodément à ce qu’elle avait à faire.
sentences.l: She went by chance to walk in the same wood where she had found Riquet with the Tuft, to muse more at ease on what she had to do.
sentences.i: By chance she went walking in the same wood where she had met Riquet with the Tuft, to ponder at her ease what she ought to do.
sentences.n: «se promener» is ‘to take a walk’. «rêver à» in 1697 is ‘to muse on, turn over in one’s mind’, not ‘to dream’. «commodement» (modern «commodément») is ‘comfortably, at leisure’. «avoir à faire» ‘to have to do’ is ‘to be obliged to do’.

sentences.t: Dans le tems qu’elle se promenoit, rêvant profondement, elle entendit un bruit sourd sous ses pieds, comme de plusieurs personnes qui vont & viennent & qui agissent.
sentences.say: Dans le temps qu’elle se promenait, rêvant profondément, elle entendit un bruit sourd sous ses pieds, comme de plusieurs personnes qui vont et viennent et qui agissent.
sentences.l: In the time that she was walking, musing deeply, she heard a muffled noise under her feet, as of several persons who go and come and who are busy.
sentences.i: While she was walking, deep in thought, she heard a muffled noise beneath her feet, as of a number of people coming and going and busy at work.
sentences.n: «Dans le tems que» ‘in the time that’ is ‘while’; the book spells «temps» both «tems» and «temps». A «bruit sourd» ‘deaf noise’ is ‘a dull, muffled sound’. «agir» ‘to act’ is here ‘to be busy’. The present tenses «vont», «viennent», «agissent» describe the kind of noise, not the moment of the story, and «profondement» is «profondément».

sentences.t: Ayant presté l’oreille plus attentivement, elle ouït que l’un disoit apporte-moy cette marmitte, l’autre donne-moy cette chaudiere, l’autre mets du bois dans ce feu.
sentences.say: Ayant prêté l’oreille plus attentivement, elle ouït que l’un disait apporte-moi cette marmite, l’autre donne-moi cette chaudière, l’autre mets du bois dans ce feu.
sentences.l: Having lent the ear more attentively, she heard that the one was saying bring me this pot, the other give me this cauldron, the other put some wood on this fire.
sentences.i: Listening more closely, she heard one voice saying, Bring me that pot, another, Hand me that cauldron, and another, Put some wood on that fire.
sentences.n: «prester l’oreille» (modern «prêter») is ‘to lend an ear, listen’, and «ouït» is the passé simple of «ouïr» ‘to hear’. The workers call to one another with «tu»: «apporte-moy», «donne-moy» and «mets» are «tu» imperatives, as fellow workers speak; the English stays ‘you’. A «marmitte» (modern «marmite») is a lidded cooking pot, and a «chaudiere» (modern «chaudière») a large cauldron. The witness sets no mark of speech around the calls, and the English adds none.

sentences.t: La terre s’ouvrit dans le même temps, & elle vit sous ses pieds comme une grande Cuisine pleine de Cuisiniers, de Marmitons & de toutes sortes d’Officiers necessaires pour faire un festin magnifique.
sentences.say: La terre s’ouvrit dans le même temps, et elle vit sous ses pieds comme une grande Cuisine pleine de Cuisiniers, de Marmitons et de toutes sortes d’Officiers nécessaires pour faire un festin magnifique.
sentences.l: The earth opened at the same time, and she saw under her feet as it were a great Kitchen full of Cooks, of Scullions and of all sorts of Officers necessary to make a magnificent feast.
sentences.i: At that moment the ground opened, and beneath her feet she saw what seemed a great kitchen full of cooks, scullions and every kind of household officer needed to prepare a splendid feast.
sentences.n: «comme» ‘as it were’ softens «une grande Cuisine»: something like a great kitchen. «Marmitons» are kitchen boys, named from the «marmite» they tended and scoured. In a great household the «Officiers» of the kitchen and the pantry, the «officiers de bouche», were the servants in charge of the food and the table. «s’ouvrit» ‘opened itself’ is passé simple, and «necessaires» lacks the accent of «nécessaires».

sentences.t: Il en sortit une bande de vingt ou trente Rotisseurs, qui allerent se camper dans une allée du bois autour d’une table fort longue, & qui tous, la lardoire à la main & la queuë de Renard sur l’oreille, se mirent à travailler en cadence au son d’une Chanson harmonieuse.
sentences.say: Il en sortit une bande de vingt ou trente Rôtisseurs, qui allèrent se camper dans une allée du bois autour d’une table fort longue, et qui tous, la lardoire à la main et la queue de Renard sur l’oreille, se mirent à travailler en cadence au son d’une Chanson harmonieuse.
sentences.l: There came out of it a band of twenty or thirty Roasters, who went to take up position in an alley of the wood around a very long table, and who all, the larding-needle in the hand and the tail of Fox over the ear, set themselves to work in cadence to the sound of a harmonious Song.
sentences.i: Out of it came a troop of twenty or thirty roasting-cooks, who went and took up their places along a walk in the wood around a very long table, and who all, larding needle in hand and fox’s tail over the ear, set to work in time to the sound of a tuneful song.
sentences.n: A «Rotisseur» (modern «rôtisseur») was a cook who roasted meat, and a «lardoire» the needle for threading strips of fat into a joint before roasting. What the fox’s tail worn over the ear signified is not certain; it seems to be a mark of their trade or of festive dress. «se camper» is ‘to take up position’, and an «allée» is a walk cut through a wood or garden. «en cadence» is ‘in rhythm’. «Il en sortit» ‘there came out of it’ is impersonal, with «en» ‘of it’, the kitchen; «allerent» (modern «allèrent») and «mirent» are passé simple, and «queuë» is «queue» ‘tail’.

sentences.t: La Princesse estonnée de ce spectacle, leur demanda pour qui ils travailloient.
sentences.say: La Princesse étonnée de ce spectacle, leur demanda pour qui ils travaillaient.
sentences.l: The Princess astonished at this spectacle, asked them for whom they were working.
sentences.i: Astonished at the sight, the Princess asked them whom they were working for.
sentences.n: «estonnée» is «étonnée» ‘astonished’, and «spectacle» is ‘sight’, anything offered to the eye. «travailloient» (modern «travaillaient») is the imperfect: what they were doing as she asked.

sentences.t: C’est, Madame, luy répondit le plus apparent de la bande, pour le Prince Riquet à la houppe, dont les nopces se feront demain.
sentences.say: C’est, Madame, lui répondit le plus apparent de la bande, pour le Prince Riquet à la houppe, dont les noces se feront demain.
sentences.l: It is, Madame, answered her the most conspicuous of the band, for the Prince Riquet with the Tuft, whose wedding will be held tomorrow.
sentences.i: It is, Madame, answered the most important-looking of the troop, for Prince Riquet with the Tuft, whose wedding is to take place tomorrow.
sentences.n: «le plus apparent» ‘the most apparent’ is ‘the most conspicuous, the one of most consequence to look at’, the leader. «nopces» is the 1697 spelling of «noces» ‘wedding’, a plural in French for a single celebration. «se feront» ‘will make themselves’ is the reflexive for a passive, ‘will be held’.

sentences.t: La Princesse, encore plus surprise qu’elle ne l’avoit esté, & se resouvenant tout à coup qu’il y avoit un an qu’à pareil jour elle avoit promis d’épouser le Prince Riquet à la houppe, elle pensa tomber de son haut.
sentences.say: La Princesse, encore plus surprise qu’elle ne l’avait été, et se ressouvenant tout à coup qu’il y avait un an qu’à pareil jour elle avait promis d’épouser le Prince Riquet à la houppe, elle pensa tomber de son haut.
sentences.l: The Princess, still more surprised than she had been, and remembering all at once that it was a year ago that on a like day she had promised to marry the Prince Riquet with the Tuft, she nearly fell from her height.
sentences.i: The Princess, even more surprised than she had been, suddenly recalled that a year ago to the day she had promised to marry Prince Riquet with the Tuft, and she almost fell over in astonishment.
sentences.n: The sentence names «La Princesse» and then takes her up again with «elle», a loose construction of spoken style that the idiomatic line tidies away. «tomber de son haut» ‘to fall from one’s full height’ is ‘to be thunderstruck’, and «pensa» is again ‘nearly’. «il y avoit un an que» ‘there had a year that’ is ‘it was a year since’. «esté» is «été» ‘been’, and «se resouvenant» is the 1697 spelling of «se ressouvenant», from «se ressouvenir», a literary word for ‘to remember, call to mind’.

sentences.t: Ce qui faisoit qu’elle ne s’en souvenoit pas, c’est que quand elle fit cette promesse, elle estoit une bête, & qu’en prenant le nouvel esprit que le Prince lui avoit donné, elle avoit oublié toutes ses sottises.
sentences.say: Ce qui faisait qu’elle ne s’en souvenait pas, c’est que quand elle fit cette promesse, elle était une bête, et qu’en prenant le nouvel esprit que le Prince lui avait donné, elle avait oublié toutes ses sottises.
sentences.l: What made that she did not remember it, it is that when she made this promise, she was a fool, and that in taking on the new wit that the Prince had given her, she had forgotten all her follies.
sentences.i: The reason she had not remembered it was that when she made the promise she was a fool, and that on receiving the new wit the Prince had given her she had forgotten all her foolishness.
sentences.n: «Ce qui … c’est que» ‘what … it is that’ throws the weight on the explanation, and «se souvenir de» is ‘to remember’. «une bête» ‘a beast’ is ‘a fool, a dunce’; here the book prints the modern «bête», elsewhere «beste». «sottises» are ‘follies, foolish things said and done’. The narrator’s reason is itself a joke: the wit that made her clever wiped out the memory of the promise that paid for it.

sentences.t: Elle n’eut pas fait trente pas en continuant sa promenade, que Riquet à la houppe se presenta à elle, brave, magnifique, & comme un Prince qui va se marier.
sentences.say: Elle n’eut pas fait trente pas en continuant sa promenade, que Riquet à la houppe se présenta à elle, brave, magnifique, et comme un Prince qui va se marier.
sentences.l: She had not taken thirty steps in continuing her walk, when Riquet with the Tuft presented himself to her, finely dressed, magnificent, and like a Prince who is going to be married.
sentences.i: She had not gone thirty paces further on her walk when Riquet with the Tuft appeared before her, in his finest clothes, magnificent, and like a prince about to be married.
sentences.n: «brave» in 1697 often means ‘finely dressed, in one’s best clothes’, and that is its sense here beside «magnifique»; neither line says ‘brave’. «faire trente pas» is ‘to take thirty steps’, and «n’eut pas fait … que» ‘had not taken … when’ follows the pattern of «n’eut pas plûtost». «se presenta» (modern «se présenta») ‘presented himself’ is ‘appeared’, and «se marier» is ‘to marry, be married’.

sentences.t: Vous me voyez, dit-il, Madame, exact à tenir ma parole, & je ne doute point que vous ne veniez ici pour executer la vostre, & me rendre, en me donnant la main, le plus heureux de tous les hommes.
sentences.say: Vous me voyez, dit-il, Madame, exact à tenir ma parole, et je ne doute point que vous ne veniez ici pour exécuter la votre, et me rendre, en me donnant la main, le plus heureux de tous les hommes.
sentences.l: You see me, said he, Madame, exact in keeping my word, and I do not doubt that you come here to carry out yours, and to make me, in giving me the hand, the happiest of all men.
sentences.i: You see me, Madame, he said, punctual in keeping my word, and I have no doubt that you have come here to keep yours and, by giving me your hand, to make me the happiest of men.
sentences.n: «exact à» is ‘punctual in, scrupulous in’. In «je ne doute point que vous ne veniez» ‘I do not doubt that you come’ the «ne» after a denied verb of doubting adds no negation, and «veniez» is subjunctive. «executer» (modern «exécuter») is ‘to carry out’, and «donner la main» ‘to give the hand’ is to give oneself in marriage. «rendre» with an adjective is ‘to make’, the verb of the fairies’ gifts.

sentences.t: Je vous avouëray franchement, répondit la Princesse, que je n’ay pas encore pris ma resolution là-dessus, & que je ne croy pas pouvoir jamais la prendre telle que vous la souhaitez.
sentences.say: Je vous avouerai franchement, répondit la Princesse, que je n’ai pas encore pris ma résolution là-dessus, et que je ne crois pas pouvoir jamais la prendre telle que vous la souhaitez.
sentences.l: I will confess to you frankly, answered the Princess, that I have not yet taken my resolution on that, and that I do not believe to be able ever to take it such as you wish it.
sentences.i: I will confess to you frankly, replied the Princess, that I have not yet made up my mind about it, and that I do not believe I can ever make it up the way you wish.
sentences.n: «avouëray» is the 1697 spelling of «avouerai» ‘I will confess’. «prendre sa resolution» (modern «résolution») is ‘to come to one’s decision’, and «là-dessus» is ‘on that’. «je ne croy pas pouvoir» ‘I do not believe to be able’ uses an infinitive where English needs ‘that I can’; «croy» is «crois», and «n’ay» is «n’ai».

sentences.t: Vous m’étonnez, Madame, lui dit Riquet à la houppe : Je le croy, dit la Princesse, & asseurement si j’avois affaire à un brutal, à un homme sans esprit, je me trouverois bien embarassée.
sentences.say: Vous m’étonnez, Madame, lui dit Riquet à la houppe : Je le crois, dit la Princesse, et assurément si j’avais affaire à un brutal, à un homme sans esprit, je me trouverais bien embarrassée.
sentences.l: You astonish me, Madame, said to her Riquet with the Tuft: I believe it, said the Princess, and assuredly if I had to do with a brute, with a man without wit, I would find myself much at a loss.
sentences.i: You astonish me, Madame, said Riquet with the Tuft. I can well believe it, said the Princess; and certainly, if I were dealing with a brute, with a man without wit, I would find myself in great difficulty.
sentences.n: A short exchange: the witness runs his line and her reply into one sentence with a colon and a capital. A «brutal» used as a noun is ‘a coarse, unfeeling man’. «avoir affaire à» is ‘to have to deal with’. «embarassée» (modern «embarrassée») is ‘in a difficulty, at a loss’, stronger than English ‘embarrassed’. «asseurement» is «assurément» ‘assuredly’, and «trouverois» is «trouverais».

sentences.t: Une Princesse n’a que sa parole, me diroit-il, & il faut que vous m’épousiez, puisque vous me l’avez promis ;
sentences.say: Une Princesse n’a que sa parole, me dirait-il, et il faut que vous m’épousiez, puisque vous me l’avez promis ;
sentences.l: A Princess has only her word, he would say to me, and it is needful that you marry me, since you have promised it to me;
sentences.i: A princess has nothing but her word, he would tell me, and you must marry me, since you promised me you would;
sentences.n: «Une Princesse n’a que sa parole» ‘a princess has only her word’ has the ring of a saying: her word is all she has, so she must keep it. «me diroit-il» (modern «me dirait-il») ‘he would say to me’ is the Princess imagining what a brute would answer. «il faut que» ‘it is needful that’ takes the subjunctive «épousiez».

sentences.t: mais, comme celuy à qui je parle est l’homme du monde qui a le plus d’esprit, je suis seure qu’il entendra raison.
sentences.say: mais, comme celui à qui je parle est l’homme du monde qui a le plus d’esprit, je suis sûre qu’il entendra raison.
sentences.l: but, as he to whom I speak is the man in the world who has the most wit, I am sure that he will hear reason.
sentences.i: but since the man I am speaking to has more wit than any man alive, I am sure he will listen to reason.
sentences.n: «celuy à qui je parle» ‘he to whom I speak’ is a courteous way of saying ‘you’ in the third person. «entendre raison» ‘to hear reason’ is ‘to listen to reason’. «seure» is the 1697 spelling of «sûre» ‘sure’, and «celuy» of «celui».

sentences.t: Vous sçavez que quand je n’estois qu’une beste, je ne pouvois neanmoins me resoudre à vous épouser, comment voulez-vous qu’ayant l’esprit que vous m’avez donné, qui me rend encore plus difficile en gens que je n’estois, je prenne aujourd’hui une resolution que je n’ay pû prendre dans ce temps-là.
sentences.say: Vous savez que quand je n’étais qu’une bête, je ne pouvais néanmoins me résoudre à vous épouser, comment voulez-vous qu’ayant l’esprit que vous m’avez donné, qui me rend encore plus difficile en gens que je n’étais, je prenne aujourd’hui une résolution que je n’ai pu prendre dans ce temps-là.
sentences.l: You know that when I was only a fool, I could not nevertheless bring myself to marry you; how do you want that, having the wit that you have given me, which makes me still more difficult in people than I was, I should take today a resolution that I could not take at that time?
sentences.i: You know that even when I was nothing but a fool I could not bring myself to marry you; how can you expect that now, with the wit you have given me, which makes me more particular about people than I was, I should come today to a decision I could not come to then?
sentences.n: «comment voulez-vous que» ‘how do you want that’ is ‘how can you expect that’, and it takes the subjunctive «prenne». The witness joins the question to the first clause with a comma and ends it with a full stop; the English gives a semicolon and a question mark, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «difficile en gens» is ‘hard to please in people’, and after «plus … que» the «ne» of «n’estois» adds no negation. «neanmoins» (modern «néanmoins») is ‘nevertheless’, and «pû» is «pu».

sentences.t: Si vous pensiez tout de bon à m’épouser, vous avez eu grand tort de m’oster ma bestise, & de me faire voir plus clair que je ne voyois.
sentences.say: Si vous pensiez tout de bon à m’épouser, vous avez eu grand tort de m’ôter ma bêtise, et de me faire voir plus clair que je ne voyais.
sentences.l: If you were thinking in good earnest of marrying me, you have been very wrong to take from me my stupidity, and to make me see more clearly than I saw.
sentences.i: If you seriously meant to marry me, you did very wrong to take away my stupidity and make me see more clearly than I did.
sentences.n: «tout de bon» is ‘in earnest’, and «avoir grand tort» ‘to have great wrong’ is ‘to be much in the wrong’. «oster» is «ôter» ‘to take away’, with the 1697 s. «voir clair» ‘to see clear’ is ‘to see clearly’, and the «ne» of «que je ne voyois» adds no negation; «voyois» is «voyais».

sentences.t: Si un homme sans esprit, répondit Riquet à la houppe, seroit bien receu, comme vous venez de le dire, à vous reprocher vostre manque de parole, pourquoi voulez-vous, Madame, que je n’en use pas de mesme, dans une chose où il y va de tout le bonheur de ma vie ;
sentences.say: Si un homme sans esprit, répondit Riquet à la houppe, serait bien reçu, comme vous venez de le dire, à vous reprocher votre manque de parole, pourquoi voulez-vous, Madame, que je n’en use pas de même, dans une chose où il y va de tout le bonheur de ma vie ;
sentences.l: If a man without wit, answered Riquet with the Tuft, would be well received, as you have just said, in reproaching you your failure of word, why do you want, Madame, that I should not act the same, in a matter where there is at stake all the happiness of my life;
sentences.i: If a man without wit, replied Riquet with the Tuft, would have good grounds, as you have just said, to reproach you with breaking your word, why, Madame, would you have me not do the same, in a matter on which the whole happiness of my life depends?
sentences.n: «seroit bien receu à» ‘would be well received in’ is ‘would have good grounds to’; «receu» is «reçu». «Si» here is ‘if it is so that’, taking up the Princess’s own imagined «me diroit-il», and so it can take the conditional «seroit», which a plain ‘if’ does not take in modern French. «en user de mesme» is ‘to act in the same way’, and «il y va de» ‘there goes of’ is ‘there is at stake’. «manque de parole» ‘lack of word’ is ‘breach of promise’.

sentences.t: est-il raisonnable que les personnes qui ont de l’esprit, soient d’une pire condition que ceux qui n’en ont pas ;
sentences.l: is it reasonable that persons who have wit, be of a worse condition than those who have none;
sentences.i: Is it reasonable that people who have wit should be worse off than those who have none?
sentences.n: «est-il raisonnable que» takes the subjunctive «soient». «d’une pire condition» ‘of a worse condition’ is ‘worse off’. «personnes» is feminine but «ceux» ‘those’ is masculine: French follows the sense, people in general.

sentences.t: le pouvez-vous prétendre, vous qui en avez tant, & qui avez tant souhaité d’en avoir ?
sentences.say: le pouvez-vous prétendre, vous qui en avez tant, et qui avez tant souhaité d’en avoir ?
sentences.l: can you claim it, you who have so much of it, and who have so much wished to have some?
sentences.i: Can you maintain that, you who have so much of it, and who so longed to have it?
sentences.n: «prétendre» is ‘to claim, maintain’, not ‘to pretend’. «le pouvez-vous prétendre» sets the pronoun before «pouvez», the 1697 order, where modern French says «pouvez-vous le prétendre». «en» ‘of it’ is wit, in both places.

sentences.t: Mais venons au fait, s’il vous plaît : A la reserve de ma laideur, y a-t-il quelque chose en moy qui vous déplaise, estes-vous malcontente de ma naissance, de mon esprit, de mon humeur, & de mes manieres ?
sentences.say: Mais venons au fait, s’il vous plaît : A la réserve de ma laideur, y a-t-il quelque chose en moi qui vous déplaise, êtes-vous malcontente de ma naissance, de mon esprit, de mon humeur, et de mes manières ?
sentences.l: But let us come to the fact, if you please: With the exception of my ugliness, is there something in me that displeases you, are you discontented with my birth, with my wit, with my temper, and with my manners?
sentences.i: But let us come to the point, if you please. Apart from my ugliness, is there anything in me that displeases you? Are you dissatisfied with my birth, my wit, my disposition or my manners?
sentences.n: «venir au fait» is ‘to come to the point’, and «A la reserve de» (modern «à la réserve de») is ‘except for’. «qui vous déplaise» is subjunctive, as a relative clause inside such a question may be. «malcontente» is an older form of «mécontente» ‘dissatisfied’. «humeur» is ‘temper, disposition’, and «naissance» ‘birth’ means rank as well as the day itself; «moy» is «moi».

sentences.t: Nullement, répondit la Princesse, j’aime en vous tout ce que vous venez de me dire.
sentences.l: Not at all, answered the Princess, I love in you all that you have just told me.
