sentences.i: Not in the least, replied the Princess; I love everything in you that you have just named.
sentences.n: «Nullement» is ‘not at all’. «j’aime» is the Princess’s first use of «aimer» ‘to love’ of Riquet, the verb her gift depends on. «venir de» with an infinitive is ‘to have just’.

sentences.t: Si cela est ainsi, reprit Riquet à la houppe, je vais estre heureux, puisque vous pouvez me rendre le plus aimable de tous les hommes.
sentences.say: Si cela est ainsi, reprit Riquet à la houppe, je vais être heureux, puisque vous pouvez me rendre le plus aimable de tous les hommes.
sentences.l: If that is so, resumed Riquet with the Tuft, I am going to be happy, since you can make me the most lovable of all men.
sentences.i: If that is so, Riquet with the Tuft went on, I shall be happy, since you can make me the most lovable of men.
sentences.n: «je vais estre» ‘I am going to be’ is the near future. «rendre» with an adjective is ‘to make’, and «aimable», as at his birth, is ‘lovable, pleasing’, here with looks in mind as well.

sentences.t: Comment cela se peut-il faire, lui dit la Princesse.
sentences.l: How can that be done? said the Princess to him.
sentences.i: How can that be? said the Princess.
sentences.n: «cela se peut-il faire» ‘can that do itself’ is the reflexive for a passive, ‘can that be done’, with «se» before «peut», the 1697 order. The witness prints no question mark, and the English supplies one.

sentences.t: Cela se fera, répondit Riquet à la houppe, si vous m’aimez assez pour souhaiter que cela soit ;
sentences.l: That will be done, answered Riquet with the Tuft, if you love me enough to wish that it be;
sentences.i: It will be done, replied Riquet with the Tuft, if you love me enough to wish it to be so;
sentences.n: «se fera» ‘will do itself’ answers her «se peut-il faire»: ‘it will be done’. «souhaiter que» ‘to wish that’ takes the subjunctive «soit» ‘be’.

sentences.t: & afin, Madame, que vous n’en doutiez pas, sçachez que la même Fée qui, au jour de ma naissance, me fit le don de pouvoir rendre spirituelle la personne qui me plairoit, vous a aussi fait le don de pouvoir rendre beau celuy que vous aimerez, & à qui vous voudrez bien faire cette faveur.
sentences.say: et afin, Madame, que vous n’en doutiez pas, sachez que la même Fée qui, au jour de ma naissance, me fit le don de pouvoir rendre spirituelle la personne qui me plairait, vous a aussi fait le don de pouvoir rendre beau celui que vous aimerez, et à qui vous voudrez bien faire cette faveur.
sentences.l: and so that, Madame, you may not doubt it, know that the same Fairy who, on the day of my birth, made me the gift of being able to make witty the person who would please me, has also made you the gift of being able to make handsome him whom you will love, and to whom you will be willing to do this favour.
sentences.i: and, so that you may not doubt it, Madame, know that the same Fairy who, on the day I was born, gave me the gift of being able to make witty whoever should please me, has also given you the gift of being able to make handsome the man you will love, and on whom you consent to bestow this favour.
sentences.n: «sçachez» is the imperative of «sçavoir» (modern «savoir»), ‘know’; «spirituelle» is ‘witty’, the adjective of «esprit», and «beau» is masculine now because the one to be made handsome is Riquet. Told again here, the two gifts have traded their verbs: at the births he was to give wit to the one he loved best and she beauty to the one who pleased her, and now his is for the one who pleases him and hers for the one she will love. «afin que» ‘so that’ takes the subjunctive «doutiez», and «n’en doutiez pas» is ‘may not doubt of it’.

sentences.t: Si la chose est ainsi, dit la Princesse, je souhaite de tout mon cœur que vous deveniez le Prince du monde le plus beau & le plus aimable ; & je vous en fais le don autant qu’il est en moy.
sentences.say: Si la chose est ainsi, dit la Princesse, je souhaite de tout mon cœur que vous deveniez le Prince du monde le plus beau et le plus aimable ; et je vous en fais le don autant qu’il est en moi.
sentences.l: If the thing is so, said the Princess, I wish with all my heart that you become the Prince of the world the most handsome and the most lovable; and I make you the gift of it as much as it is in me.
sentences.i: If that is so, said the Princess, I wish with all my heart that you may become the handsomest and most lovable prince in the world; and I bestow the gift on you, as far as it lies in my power.
sentences.n: «deveniez» is subjunctive after «souhaiter que». «le Prince du monde le plus beau» ‘the Prince of the world the most handsome’ sets the superlative after «du monde». «je vous en fais le don» ‘I make you the gift of it’ takes up the fairies’ «faire le don», and «autant qu’il est en moy» ‘as much as it is in me’ is ‘as far as lies in my power’. «cœur» ‘heart’ is printed with the joined œ.

sentences.t: La Princesse n’eut pas plustost prononcé ces paroles, que Riquet à la houppe parut à ses yeux, l’homme du monde le plus beau, le mieux fait, & le plus aimable qu’elle eust jamais vû.
sentences.say: La Princesse n’eut pas plutôt prononcé ces paroles, que Riquet à la houppe parut à ses yeux, l’homme du monde le plus beau, le mieux fait, et le plus aimable qu’elle eût jamais vu.
sentences.l: The Princess had not sooner pronounced these words, than Riquet with the Tuft appeared to her eyes, the man in the world the most handsome, the best made, and the most lovable that she had ever seen.
sentences.i: No sooner had the Princess spoken these words than Riquet with the Tuft appeared before her eyes as the handsomest, best-made and most lovable man she had ever seen.
sentences.n: «n’eut pas plustost … que» is ‘no sooner … than’ once more, with yet another spelling, «plustost». «parut» is the passé simple of «paraître» ‘to appear’. «eust jamais vû» (modern «eût jamais vu») is the pluperfect subjunctive after a superlative: the handsomest she had ever seen. «le mieux fait» ‘the best made’ answers the «mal fait» of Riquet’s birth.

sentences.t: Quelques-uns asseurent que ce ne furent point les charmes de la Fée qui opererent, mais que l’amour seul fit cette Metamorphose.
sentences.say: Quelques-uns assurent que ce ne furent point les charmes de la Fée qui opérèrent, mais que l’amour seul fit cette Métamorphose.
sentences.l: Some assure that it was not at all the charms of the fairy that worked, but that love alone made this Metamorphosis.
sentences.i: Some maintain that it was not the fairy’s spells that did it at all, but that love alone worked this transformation.
sentences.n: «charmes» here are ‘spells, enchantments’, the word’s old sense, from Latin «carmen» ‘song, incantation’. «opererent» (modern «opérèrent») is ‘worked, took effect’. A «Metamorphose» (modern «métamorphose») is a change of form, the word of Ovid’s «Métamorphoses»; the narrator now offers a second account of what happened. In «ce ne furent point … qui» ‘it was not … that’ the verb «être» is plural to agree with its plural noun.

sentences.t: Ils disent que la Princesse, ayant fait reflexion sur la perseverance de son Amant, sur sa discretion, & sur toutes les bonnes qualitez de son ame & de son esprit, ne vit plus la difformité de son corps, ny la laideur de son visage, que sa bosse ne lui sembla plus que le bon air d’un homme qui fait le gros dos ;
sentences.say: Ils disent que la Princesse, ayant fait réflexion sur la persévérance de son Amant, sur sa discrétion, et sur toutes les bonnes qualités de son âme et de son esprit, ne vit plus la difformité de son corps, ni la laideur de son visage, que sa bosse ne lui sembla plus que le bon air d’un homme qui fait le gros dos ;
sentences.l: They say that the Princess, having reflected on the perseverance of her Suitor, on his discretion, and on all the good qualities of his soul and of his wit, no longer saw the deformity of his body, nor the ugliness of his face, that his hump no longer seemed to her anything but the fine air of a man who makes the big back;
sentences.i: They say that the Princess, having reflected on her suitor’s constancy, on his discretion and on all the good qualities of his soul and mind, no longer saw the deformity of his body or the ugliness of his face; that his hump seemed to her no more than the fine bearing of a man who carries himself with an air of consequence;
sentences.n: «son Amant» is ‘her suitor’, the man who loves her and seeks her hand; in 1697 the word says nothing of a love affair, and neither line says ‘lover’. «faire reflexion sur» (modern «réflexion») is ‘to reflect on’. «esprit» here is ‘mind’ as well as ‘wit’, beside «ame» (modern «âme») ‘soul’: the literal line keeps the tale’s ‘wit’, the idiomatic line says ‘mind’. «faire le gros dos» ‘to make the big back’ seems to have meant ‘to give oneself airs, puff oneself up’, the way a cat arches its back, though the exact sense here is not certain. «qualitez» is «qualités», «ny» is «ni», and «ne … plus que» is ‘no longer anything but’.

sentences.t: & qu’au lieu que jusqu’à lors elle l’avoit vû boitter effroyablement, elle ne lui trouva plus qu’un certain air penché qui la charmoit ;
sentences.say: et qu’au lieu que jusqu’à lors elle l’avait vu boiter effroyablement, elle ne lui trouva plus qu’un certain air penché qui la charmait ;
sentences.l: and that whereas until then she had seen him limp frightfully, she no longer found in him anything but a certain leaning air that charmed her;
sentences.i: and that, whereas until then she had seen him limp dreadfully, she now found in him nothing but a certain languid tilt, which charmed her;
sentences.n: «au lieu que» ‘instead of that’ is ‘whereas’. «jusqu’à lors» is the older spelling of «jusqu’alors» ‘until then’, and «boitter» of «boiter» ‘to limp’. An «air penché» ‘a leaning air’ seems to have been a deliberate, languid pose, the body or head gracefully inclined, affected in fashionable company: what was a limp now looks like a fashion. «charmoit» (modern «charmait») is ‘charmed, delighted’.

sentences.t: ils disent encore que ses yeux qui estoient louches, ne luy en parurent que plus brillans, que leur déreglement passa dans son esprit pour la marque d’un violent excez d’amour, & qu’enfin son gros nez rouge eut pour elle quelque chose de Martial & d’Heroïque ?
sentences.say: ils disent encore que ses yeux qui étaient louches, ne lui en parurent que plus brillants, que leur dérèglement passa dans son esprit pour la marque d’un violent excès d’amour, et qu’enfin son gros nez rouge eut pour elle quelque chose de Martial et d’Héroïque ?
sentences.l: they say further that his eyes, which were squinting, appeared to her only the more brilliant for it, that their disorder passed in her mind for the mark of a violent excess of love, and that finally his big red nose had for her something Martial and Heroic.
sentences.i: they say too that his squinting eyes only seemed the brighter to her for it, that their straying passed in her mind for the sign of a violent excess of love, and that, last of all, his big red nose had something soldierly and heroic about it for her.
sentences.n: «louches» is ‘squinting, cross-eyed’. In «ne luy en parurent que plus brillans» ‘appeared to her only the more brilliant for it’, «en» ‘for it’ makes the squint itself the cause. «brillans» drops the t of the plural (modern «brillants»), «déreglement» is «dérèglement» ‘disorder’, and «excez» is «excès» ‘excess’. «Martial» is ‘warlike, soldierly’, a quality to be prized in a prince. The witness ends this statement with a question mark where the sense wants a full stop; the English ends with a full stop, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «passa dans son esprit pour» ‘passed in her mind for’ is ‘seemed to her to be’; here «esprit» can only be ‘mind’, not the tale’s ‘wit’.

sentences.t: Quoy qu’il en soit, la Princesse luy promit sur-le-champ de l’épouser, pourvû qu’il en obtînt le consentement du Roy son pere.
sentences.say: Quoi qu’il en soit, la Princesse lui promit sur-le-champ de l’épouser, pourvu qu’il en obtînt le consentement du Roi son père.
sentences.l: Whatever may be of it, the Princess promised him on the spot to marry him, provided that he obtained for it the consent of the King her father.
sentences.i: However that may be, the Princess promised on the spot to marry him, provided he obtained the consent of the King her father.
sentences.n: «Quoy qu’il en soit» (modern «quoi qu’il en soit») ‘whatever may be of it’ is ‘however that may be’: the narrator leaves the two accounts side by side. «sur-le-champ» ‘on the field’ is ‘at once’. «pourvû que» ‘provided that’ takes the subjunctive, here the imperfect subjunctive «obtînt», printed with its circumflex. A princess could not marry without the King’s consent.

sentences.t: Le Roy, ayant sçû que sa fille avait beaucoup d’estime pour Riquet à la houppe, qu’il connoissoit d’ailleurs pour un Prince trés-spirituel & trés-sage, le receut avec plaisir pour son gendre.
sentences.say: Le Roi, ayant su que sa fille avait beaucoup d’estime pour Riquet à la houppe, qu’il connaissait d’ailleurs pour un Prince très-spirituel et très-sage, le reçut avec plaisir pour son gendre.
sentences.l: The King, having come to know that his daughter had much esteem for Riquet with the Tuft, whom he knew besides for a very witty and very wise Prince, received him with pleasure for his son-in-law.
sentences.i: The King, on hearing that his daughter held Riquet with the Tuft in high esteem, and knowing him besides to be a most witty and wise prince, gladly accepted him as his son-in-law.
sentences.n: «ayant sçû» (modern «ayant su») ‘having known’ is ‘having found out’. «estime» is ‘esteem, high regard’, a word of respect rather than passion. «connoistre pour» ‘to know for’ is ‘to know to be’. The witness prints «avait» in the modern spelling beside «connoissoit» in the old; both are imperfects. «receut» is «reçut» ‘received’, and «trés-» is «très» ‘very’ joined by a hyphen.

sentences.t: Dés le lendemain les nopces furent faites, ainsi que Riquet à la houppe l’avoit prévû, & selon les ordres qu’il en avoit donnez long-temps auparavant.
sentences.say: Dès le lendemain les noces furent faites, ainsi que Riquet à la houppe l’avait prévu, et selon les ordres qu’il en avait donnez longtemps auparavant.
sentences.l: From the next day the wedding was held, just as Riquet with the Tuft had foreseen it, and according to the orders that he had given for it a long time before.
sentences.i: The very next day the wedding took place, just as Riquet with the Tuft had foreseen, and according to the orders he had given for it long before.
sentences.n: «Dés le lendemain» (modern «dès le lendemain») is ‘the very next day’. «les nopces furent faites» ‘the wedding was made’ is the passé simple of the passive. «prévû» is «prévu» ‘foreseen’, and «donnez» is «donnés» ‘given’, a participle in «-ez»; «long-temps» is «longtemps», with a hyphen. The kitchen in the wood was carrying out those orders.

sentences.t: MORALITÉ.
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: «Moralité» is ‘moral’. Each tale in the book closes with a moral in verse, and this one has two; they belong to the tale as much as the story does.

sentences.t:
Ce que l'on voit dans cet écrit
Est moins un conte en l’air que la verité même ;
sentences.say:
Ce que l'on voit dans cet écrit,
Est moins un conte en l’air que la vérité même ;
sentences.l:
What one sees in this writing
Is less a tale in the air than the truth itself;
sentences.i:
What this story shows
Is less an idle fancy than the very truth;
sentences.n: «un conte en l’air» ‘a tale in the air’ is ‘an idle, groundless tale’. «l’on» is «on» ‘one’ with an «l’» added for the sound after «que»; the witness prints its apostrophe straight here, and Lectorium keeps it. «verité» lacks the accent of «vérité», and «même» after a noun is ‘itself, very’. The morals are in rhymed lines of different lengths; the English follows them line for line and does not rhyme.

sentences.t:
Tout est beau dans ce que l'on aime,
Tout ce qu’on aime a de l’esprit.
sentences.l:
All is beautiful in what one loves,
All that one loves has wit.
sentences.i:
Everything is beautiful in what we love,
And whatever we love has wit.
sentences.n: The two halves of the tale meet in these two lines: «beau» ‘beautiful’ was the elder princess’s gift and «esprit» ‘wit’ was Riquet’s. «a de l’esprit» ‘has some wit’ is ‘is witty’. The first line again prints the apostrophe of «l’on» straight, and the second prints «qu’on» with a curly one; Lectorium keeps both as printed.

sentences.t: Autre Moralité.
sentences.l: ANOTHER MORAL

sentences.t:
Dans un objet où la Nature
Aura mis de beaux traits & la vive peinture
D’un teint où jamais l’Art ne sçauroit arriver,
Tous ces dons pourront moins pour rendre un cœur sensible
Qu’un seul agrément invisible
Que l’Amour y fera trouver.
sentences.say:
Dans un objet où la Nature,
Aura mis de beaux traits et la vive peinture,
D’un teint où jamais l’Art ne saurait arriver,
Tous ces dons pourront moins pour rendre un cœur sensible,
Qu’un seul agrément invisible,
Que l’Amour y fera trouver.
sentences.l:
In an object where Nature
Will have put fine features and the lively painting
Of a complexion where never Art could reach,
All these gifts will be able to do less to make a heart feeling
Than a single invisible charm
That Love will make one find there.
sentences.i:
In one on whom Nature
Has bestowed fine features and the living colour
Of a complexion no art could ever match,
All these gifts will do less to move a heart
Than one unseen charm
That Love will cause it to find there.
sentences.n: An «objet» in the love language of the time is ‘the beloved’, the person on whom love is fixed. «aura mis» ‘will have put’ is the future perfect, of what is supposed to be the case. «peinture» ‘painting’ is the colouring of the face, and «l’Art» is art as against «la Nature», perhaps with the art of paint and powder in mind. «ne sçauroit» (modern «ne saurait») ‘would not know how to’ is ‘could not’. «pouvoir moins pour» is ‘to do less towards’, and «rendre un cœur sensible» ‘to make a heart feeling’ is ‘to make a heart open to love’. «agrément» is ‘charm, grace’, and «y» ‘there’ is in the beloved.
